rows.msg: Do you reckon the Murrumbidgee general security allocation will get to 100% by the end of the season?
rows.text:
Short version: possible, but on the current signals it's not where the odds sit. I can only give you ranges and drivers here, not a call.

Waterfind's house outlook for Murrumbidgee general security (generated 1 Aug 2026) puts the likely end-of-season final between about **44.5% and 78.5%** (middle half of 11 similar past seasons), with roughly 32-81% covering 8 in 10. 100% shows up only in the wetter analogues, not the base case. That card's allocation input is stale (announced 32% at month 4, as at 1 Oct 2025), so treat it as historical shape rather than today's number.

Two live drivers point the same way:
- Opening was weak this season, and carryover was flagged under ~15% (NSW opening announcement, as at 8 Jul 2026).
- BOM/DPIRD have El Niño developing over Jun-Aug 2026 (~80%) and strengthening, which historically means a slower allocation ratchet and firmer temp-water prices in the southern Basin (issued 7 Jun 2026).

One thing to check: the opening GS figure isn't clean in my snapshot. One source shows a 0% opening, another reports 40%. The authoritative forward read is NSW DCCEEW's fortnightly Murrumbidgee water allocation statement (latest 15 Jul 2026), which carries dry/median/wet scenario projections. Verify there before acting.

General information only, not financial or trading advice. Want me to pull the temp-price scenario bands alongside this?

Sources:
- [NSW DCCEEW water allocation statements](https://www.water.dcceew.nsw.gov.au/our-work/allocations-and-availability/allocations/water-allocation-statements)

rows.text:
For your main parcel, the VIC Murray high-reliability shares (your 250 ML in the Dartmouth-to-Barmah zone), the house outlook has it finishing the season at **100%**.

Per the Waterfind house card (generated 1 Aug 2026), HRWS was already announced at 100% at month 5 of the season (as at 17 Nov 2025). Across 14 similar past seasons the final has typically landed at 100% (the whole middle half), with 100-120% covering 8 of 10 (the upside reflects carryover parking, not fresh allocation).

The climate backdrop is the watch item: BOM/NSW DPIRD (7 Jun 2026) had ENSO neutral but El Niño developing over June-August at ~80% likelihood and persisting to at least November. El Niño leans drier in the southern Basin, but high-reliability shares are the last class to be trimmed, so 100% is a firm expectation. It's your low-reliability parcels (the Barmah-to-SA LRWS and Goulburn 1A LRWS) where a drier run would actually bite the final number.

Want me to pull the LRWS outlook for those, or the SA Murray parcel?

General information only, from historical Waterfind data, not a prediction or financial advice. The allocation figures are a snapshot (stale as at Nov 2025) so confirm against the current Northern Victoria Resource Manager determination before acting.

rows.msg: What are the chances we see a full allocation again next season?
rows.text:
For your main parcel, VIC Murray high-reliability water shares (Dartmouth to Barmah), the odds of getting back to 100% are historically strong, but next season's opening is soft and the climate signal leans against a quick climb.

Here's the house outlook (generated 1 Aug 2026), quoted as historical frequencies, not a forecast:

- On 14 comparable past seasons, HRWS finals landed at 100% in effectively all of them (distribution min 95%, p10 through p90 all 100%). Across all 31 seasons in the series the base rate is similar: p10 95%, median 100%, with wetter years running above 100% on carryover/spill.
- The current season (2026-27) opened at just **29%** for VIC Murray HRWS as at 1 July 2026 (NVRM opening determination) — normal, since determinations start low each July and ratchet up.
- Climate is the swing factor: SOI sat at -14.5 for June 2026 and BOM/DPIRD (7 Jun 2026) had El Niño developing (~80-90% likelihood) and persisting to at least November. El Niño leans drier over the southern Basin, which historically means a slower climb, not necessarily a lower final for high-reliability shares.

So the honest read: HRWS reaching full is the historical norm and reliability class works in your favour, but the dry lean means it may get there later, and a genuinely dry run is the tail that keeps it short. Verify against the current NVRM determination before acting.

General information only, not financial or trading advice. Want me to pull the same picture for your Goulburn or low-reliability parcels?

rows.msg: Is temporary water going to get more expensive after Christmas?
rows.text:
Short answer: the house view leans that way, but it's a lean not a lock, and it's about drivers rather than a firm number.

Two things point to firmer temporary prices across the southern connected system into the new year:

- **Seasonal demand.** In the VIC Murray temp market, prices normally climb from spring into the mid-summer irrigation peak (roughly Jan-Feb) as unallocated water tightens, before easing late season. After Christmas is usually the dearer part of the year.
- **Climate.** Waterfind's outlook for your main zone (6 VIC Murray, Dartmouth-Barmah, generated 1 Aug 2026) cites the Bureau/NSW DPIRD update of 7 Jun 2026: ENSO neutral in early June but models strongly agreeing El Niño develops over Jun-Aug (~80%) and likely persists past November (~90%). El Niño summers lean drier over the southern Basin, which historically means a slower allocation ratchet-up and firmer temporary prices.

Against that, VIC Murray high-reliability allocation was already at 100% (as at 17 Nov 2025), and storages are middling (VIC dams ~50% full, June 2026 snapshot), so it's not a drought-squeeze setup.

For scale, the outlook's historical December temp band (median-season) sits around **$132-$438/ML, median ~$367**, but that's a past-frequency range as at 30 Jan 2026, not a prediction, and the price data behind it is stale (183 days old).

General information only, not personal financial or trading advice. The bands are historical frequencies, not forecasts, and the market can move outside them. Want me to pull the live order book and recent settled band for a specific zone so you're working off current figures?

rows.msg: Is my entitlement likely to be worth more in five years than it is now?
rows.text:
Short version: no one can tell you, and the honest signals point both ways. Here's what the data shows for your main entitlement, the VIC Murray high-reliability parcel (250 ML, Dartmouth to Barmah).

The last settled annual median Waterfind recorded for that pool was **$3,850/ML** (as at Jan 2024 — that permanent-sale series is stale, so treat it as a historical anchor). Growth history is genuinely mixed: the full-series trend runs about +10.6%/yr and the trailing 10-year about +8%/yr, but the trailing 5 years is roughly -3.4%/yr. So the long climb has flattened recently.

Two ways of extending it:

```chart
{"type":"line","title":"VIC Murray High-R entitlement — median $/ML, history + scenarios","unit":"$/ML","x":["2019","2021","2023","2024","+1yr","+3yr","+5yr"],"series":[{"name":"Settled median (history)","data":[4550,4600,2900,3850,null,null,null]},{"name":"Trend extrapolation (~6%/yr)","data":[null,null,null,3850,4725,5322,5995]},{"name":"Zero-drift central","data":[null,null,null,3850,3850,3850,null]}],"band":{"name":"Trend p25–p75","low":[null,null,null,3850,3855,4252,4674],"high":[null,null,null,3850,5792,6661,7690]}}
```

The trend model puts 5-year central near **$5,995/ML** (p25-p75 roughly $4,700-$7,700); the zero-drift model assumes no gain at all and just widens the spread. The difference is entirely which past window you trust.

Drivers that will actually decide it: Basin Plan/SDL and buyback policy (the big structural risk a price trend can't capture), carryover-rule changes, and the drier El Niño lean the Bureau flagged for 2026 (models ~80%+ into spring), which tends to firm water values. General information only, not personal financial or trading advice — whether to hold or sell is your and your broker's call. Want me to pull the current live permanent order book for that zone to replace the stale anchor?

Sources: Waterfind house outlook (generated 1 Aug 2026); entitlement value series as at 5 Jan 2024; Bureau of Meteorology / NSW DPIRD seasonal update, 7 Jun 2026.

rows.msg: Would you expect permanent water values to keep climbing the way they have?
rows.text:
Short answer: the steep climb is a decade-old story, not a current one. For your main parcel (Victorian Murray high-reliability, Dartmouth-to-Barmah), settled permanent values roughly tripled from 2015 to 2019, then flattened and drifted sideways. The trailing 5-year growth rate is actually slightly negative (about -3.4%/yr), versus roughly +8%/yr over 10 years. So the trend that built most of the value has already stalled.

```chart
{"type":"line","title":"VIC Murray (Dartmouth-Barmah) High-R — median settled permanent price","unit":"$/ML","x":["2015","2016","2017","2018","2019","2020","2021","2022","2023","2024"],"series":[{"name":"Median settled","data":[1925,2650,2600,3700,4550,4425,4600,4140,2900,3850]}]}```

What's actually driving the level, and why "keep climbing" isn't a given:
- Permanent values are set more by long-run reliability and scarcity expectations than by any one season. High-reliability shares hold value because delivery is dependable.
- The big structural swing factor is policy: Basin Plan water recovery, any renewed Commonwealth buyback, SDL and carryover rule changes can move the level well outside anything a price trend would predict, up or down.
- Horticulture demand (almonds, permanent plantings downstream) has underpinned the floor; a plateau in new plantings takes pressure off.

Two cautions: this series is nominal and only runs to January 2024, so it predates the current season's conditions and any recent buyback news. Worth checking recent comparable sales before you lean on it.

General information only, not personal financial or trading advice.

rows.msg: When will the government run the next buyback tender in the Basin?
rows.text:
No firm date has been published for the next tender. Buybacks now run as rolling Expression of Interest (EOI) rounds under DCCEEW's Restoring Our Rivers Voluntary Water Purchase Program (the 1,500 GL cap was repealed by the Water Amendment (Restoring Our Rivers) Act 2023), not on a fixed tender calendar.

Where things stand as of mid-2026:
- **Northern Basin EOI** (ATM_2026_5959) ran 5 March to 30 April 2026 and was still under evaluation in July 2026. Results will shape further recovery toward the 450 GL target.
- **Southern connected system** (your patch): two procurements, "Remaining Southern Connected Basin catchments" and "Large portfolios of water," are closed to new EOIs but purchasing under them is continuing. There's no announced opening date for a fresh southern round.

DCCEEW says future purchasing will be informed by the northern evaluation, so the next opening is contingent, not scheduled. Watch the department's "Government water purchasing" and AusTender pages for the announcement, and note the southern connected purchase limit of 300 GL still frames how much can be bought there.

Want me to pull recent southern-connected allocation-price context so you can see how an announced round might move your clients' market?

Sources:
- [Voluntary Water Purchase Program for the 450 GL — DCCEEW](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/water/policy/water-recovery/government-water-purchasing/voluntary-restoring-our-rivers)
- [Australian Government water purchasing in the Murray–Darling Basin — DCCEEW](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/water/policy/water-recovery/government-water-purchasing)

rows.msg: Explain the difference between general security and high security entitlements.
rows.text:
High security and general security are two reliability classes of NSW water access licence. High security entitlements get their allocation first and almost every year, so they suit permanent plantings that need water no matter the season. General security sits lower in the priority order, so its yearly allocation swings widely with storage and inflows, often well below 100% in dry years. That reliability gap is why high security trades at a premium.

Want the Victorian equivalent (high vs low reliability shares) or current allocation levels for a specific valley?
